title: Amazing grace (Newton, 1779)
hook: 'twas grace that taught my heart to fear, and grace my fears relieved
tomorrow: a song asks you straight out: were you there when…?

segments.voice: Poets, preachers and hymns: help pulled him out; the trumpets sounded; I felt my heart; I am thine; my soul, my life, my all. And yesterday, And can it be: my chains fell off. Six lines. Today's hymn looks back over a road like that.
screen: `MY CHAINS FELL OFF.` → `A WEEK OF POETS AND HYMNS.`

segments.voice: The end-of-year slideshow: freshman photos, bad haircuts, the trip, the hard semester, and then a final slide that just says what's next. Looking back and looking ahead in one breath. A hymn printed in Olney Hymns under the title Faith's Review and Expectation does exactly that. You know it by its first two words: amazing grace.
screen: `THE END-OF-YEAR SLIDESHOW.` → `FAITH'S REVIEW AND EXPECTATION.` → `AMAZING GRACE.`

segments.voice: John Newton wrote it, and the title is a map. The review comes first: "I once was lost, but now am found, Was blind, but now I see." Then a line that surprises people: "'Twas grace that taught my heart to fear, And grace my fears reliev'd." The same grace does both: first it shows you where you really stand, then it calms you there. Then the expectation: "Thro' many dangers, toils and snares, I have already come; 'Tis grace has brought me safe thus far, And grace will lead me home." Thus far is a Bible word in disguise. Newton set the hymn beside King David's prayer: "Who am I, O LORD God, and what is mine house, that thou hast brought me hitherto?" Hitherto means thus far. So the hymn is David's question, sung: look how far I've been brought, and the same hands will bring me the rest of the way.
screen: `REVIEW: LOST, THEN FOUND.` · `GRACE TAUGHT FEAR, THEN RELIEVED IT.` · `THUS FAR: DAVID'S HITHERTO.` · `EXPECTATION: HOME.` · then, large: `GRACE WILL LEAD ME HOME.`

segments.voice: Sing one verse, out loud or under your breath, any tune you know: 'tis grace has brought me safe thus far, and grace will lead me home. If singing isn't yours, say it slowly instead. Then sit with the two halves: how far you've come, and where you're headed.
Amazing grace. Newton's hymn of review and expectation: lost and found, fear taught and relieved, and a road that ends at home.
Your line: grace will lead me home. Thus far, and the rest of the way. Two weeks, sung through.

Newton quoted from Olney Hymns (1779), Book 1, hymn 41, headed 'Faith's review and expectation' with 1 Chronicles 17:16-17. Confirm wording: the original verse 3 reads ''Tis grace has brought me safe thus far' in some printings and ''Tis grace hath brought me safe thus far' in others.
